The **Socialist Party** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Parti socialiste_[[paʁti sɔsjalist]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")**PS**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-10)) is a [centre-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-left_politics "Centre-left politics")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-Statham2007-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-Topaloff2012-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-Guardian-3) to [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-De_La_Cerda_2023-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-Public_Senat_2022-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-France_Info_2018-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-Jean_Jaures_2023-7) [political party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_France "List of political parties in France") in France. It holds [social democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-11) and [pro-European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-Europeanism "Pro-Europeanism") views.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-13) The PS was for decades the largest party of the "[French Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Left "French Left")" and used to be one of the two major political parties under the [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fifth_Republic "French Fifth Republic"), along with the [Rally for the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_for_the_Republic "Rally for the Republic") in the late 20th century, and with the [Union for a Popular Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_for_a_Popular_Movement "Union for a Popular Movement") in the early 2000s. It is currently led by First Secretary [Olivier Faure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Faure "Olivier Faure"). The PS is a member of the [Party of European Socialists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_of_European_Socialists "Party of European Socialists"), [Progressive Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Alliance "Progressive Alliance") and [Socialist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_International "Socialist International").
The PS was founded in 1969 from a merger of the [French Section of the Workers' International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International "French Section of the Workers' International") (SFIO), the [Convention of Republican Institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_of_Republican_Institutions "Convention of Republican Institutions") led by [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand"), and other groups. In the 1970s, the PS surpassed the [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party")'s share of the left-wing vote. It first won power in 1981, when Mitterrand was elected [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France"). The PS achieved a governing majority in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_National_Assembly "French National Assembly") from 1981 to 1986, and again from 1988 to 1993. PS leader [Lionel Jospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin") lost his bid to succeed Mitterrand as president in 1995 to conservative [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac "Jacques Chirac"), but he served as [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_France "Prime Minister of France") in a [cohabitation government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohabitation_\(government\) "Cohabitation \(government\)") from 1997 to 2002, when he was again defeated by Chirac in the presidential election.
In the [2007 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_French_presidential_election "2007 French presidential election"), the PS's candidate, [Ségolène Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9gol%C3%A8ne_Royal "Ségolène Royal"), was defeated by conservative [Nicolas Sarkozy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Sarkozy "Nicolas Sarkozy"). In 2012, [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), the leader of the party from 1997 to 2008, was elected president, and the party also won a governing majority. During his term, Hollande battled with high unemployment, [multiple Jihadi terrorist attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_terrorist_incidents_in_France "List of terrorist incidents in France"), poor opinion ratings and a splinter group of Socialist MPs known as _frondeurs_ (rebels). Facing the emergence of centrist [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron") and left-winger [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon"), PS candidate [Benoît Hamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon") finished 5th in the [2017 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_presidential_election "2017 French presidential election"). The PS also declined to the 4th largest party in the [2017 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_legislative_election "2017 French legislative election"), and to the 6th largest in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_French_legislative_election "2022 French legislative election").
Several figures who acted at the international level have also been members of the PS, including [Jacques Delors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Delors "Jacques Delors"), who was the [president of the European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_European_Commission "President of the European Commission") from 1985 to 1994 and the first person to serve three terms in that office;[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-europa1-14) [Dominique Strauss-Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn"), who was the [managing director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managing_director "Managing director") of the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") from 2007 to 2011;[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-15) and [Pascal Lamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_Lamy "Pascal Lamy"), who was [Director-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director-General_of_the_World_Trade_Organization "Director-General of the World Trade Organization") of the [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization") from 2005 to 2013.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-16) Party membership has declined precipitously, to a low of 22,000 members in 2021,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-membership-17) down from 173,486 members in 2012,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-18) although it claimed 47,000 members in 2024,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-19) recovering to its standing around 2016, when it had 42,300 members.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-2017-members-20)
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
### French socialist movement and the SFIO
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: French socialist movement and the SFIO")]
Main article: [French Section of the Workers' International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International "French Section of the Workers' International")
The defeat of the [Paris Commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Commune "Paris Commune") (1871) greatly reduced the power and influence of the socialist movements in France. Its leaders were killed or exiled. France's first socialist party, the [Federation of the Socialist Workers of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_the_Socialist_Workers_of_France "Federation of the Socialist Workers of France") (FTSF), was founded in 1879. It was characterised as "possibilist" because it promoted [gradual reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformism "Reformism"). Two parties split off from it: in 1882, the [French Workers' Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Workers'_Party "French Workers' Party") (POF) of [Jules Guesde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Guesde "Jules Guesde") and [Paul Lafargue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lafargue "Paul Lafargue") (the son-in-law of [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx "Karl Marx")), then in 1890 the [Revolutionary Socialist Workers' Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Socialist_Workers'_Party_\(France\) "Revolutionary Socialist Workers' Party \(France\)") (POSR) of [Jean Allemane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Allemane "Jean Allemane"). At the same time, the heirs of [Louis Auguste Blanqui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Auguste_Blanqui "Louis Auguste Blanqui"), a symbol of the French revolutionary tradition, created the [Central Revolutionary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Revolutionary_Committee "Central Revolutionary Committee") (CRC) led by [Édouard Vaillant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Vaillant "Édouard Vaillant"). There were also some declared socialist deputies such as [Alexandre Millerand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Millerand "Alexandre Millerand") and [Jean Jaurès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Jaur%C3%A8s "Jean Jaurès") who did not belong to any party.
In 1899, the participation of Millerand in [Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Waldeck-Rousseau "Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau")'s cabinet caused a debate about socialist participation in a "bourgeois government". Three years later, Jaurès, Allemane and the possibilists founded the possibilist [French Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Socialist_Party_\(1902\) "French Socialist Party \(1902\)"), which supported participation in government, while Guesde and Vaillant formed the [Socialist Party of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_of_France_\(1902\) "Socialist Party of France \(1902\)"), which opposed such co-operation. In 1905, during the [Globe Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Congress "Globe Congress"), the two groups merged in the [French Section of the Workers' International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International "French Section of the Workers' International") (SFIO). Leader of the parliamentary group and director of the party paper _[L'Humanité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Humanit%C3%A9 "L'Humanité")_
The party was hemmed in between the [middle-class liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_elite "Liberal elite") of the [Radical Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Party_\(France\) "Radical Party \(France\)") and the revolutionary [syndicalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicalism "Syndicalism") who dominated the trade unions. Furthermore, the goal to rally all the Socialists in one single party was partially reached: some elects refused to join the SFIO and created the [Republican-Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican-Socialist_Party "Republican-Socialist Party"), which supported socialist participation in liberal governments. Together with the Radicals, who wished to install [laicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C3%AFcit%C3%A9 "Laïcité"), the SFIO was a component of the Left Block (_[Bloc des gauches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloc_des_gauches "Bloc des gauches")_) without to sit in the government. In 1906, the [General Confederation of Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Confederation_of_Labour_\(France\) "General Confederation of Labour \(France\)") trade union claimed its independence from all political parties.
The French socialists were strongly anti-war, but following the assassination of Jaurès in 1914 they were unable to resist the wave of militarism which followed the outbreak of World War I. They suffered a severe split over participation in the wartime government of national unity. In 1919 the anti-war socialists were heavily defeated in elections. In 1920, during the [Tours Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tours_Congress "Tours Congress"), the majority and left wing of the party broke away and formed the [French Section of the Communist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") (SFIC) to join the [Third International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comintern "Comintern") founded by [Vladimir Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin "Vladimir Lenin"). The right wing, led by [Léon Blum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Blum "Léon Blum"), kept the "old house" and remained in the SFIO.
In 1924 and in 1932, the Socialists joined with the Radicals in the Coalition of the Left (_[Cartel des Gauches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartel_des_Gauches "Cartel des Gauches")_), but refused to join the non-Socialist governments led by the Radicals [Édouard Herriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Herriot "Édouard Herriot") and [Édouard Daladier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Daladier "Édouard Daladier"). These governments failed because the Socialists and the Radicals could not agree on economic policy, and also because the Communists, following the [policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Period "Third Period") laid down by the Soviet Union, refused to support governments presiding over capitalist economies. The question of the possibility of a government participation with Radicals caused the split of "[neosocialists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neosocialism "Neosocialism")" at the beginning of the 1930s. They merged with the [Republican-Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican-Socialist_Party "Republican-Socialist Party") in the [Socialist Republican Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republican_Union "Socialist Republican Union").
In 1934, the Communists changed their line, and the four left-wing parties came together in the [Popular Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Front_\(France\) "Popular Front \(France\)"), which won the 1936 elections and brought Blum to power as France's first SFIO prime minister. Indeed, for the first time in its history, the SFIO obtained more votes and seats than the Radical Party and it formed the central axis of a left-wing parliamentary majority. Within a year, however, his government collapsed over economic policy and also over the issue of the [Spanish Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War "Spanish Civil War"). The fall of the Popular Front caused a new split from the SFIO, with the departure of the left wing of the party, led by [Marceau Pivert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marceau_Pivert "Marceau Pivert"), to the [Workers and Peasants' Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers_and_Peasants'_Socialist_Party "Workers and Peasants' Socialist Party"). The demoralised Left fell apart and was unable to resist the collapse of the [French Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Third_Republic "French Third Republic") after the military defeat of 1940.
After the liberation of France in 1944, the SFIO re-emerged in a coalition with a powerful [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") (PCF), which became the largest left-wing party, and the [Christian democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_democracy "Christian democracy") [Popular Republican Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Republican_Movement "Popular Republican Movement") (MRP). This alliance installed the main elements of the French [welfare state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state "Welfare state") and the [French Fourth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fourth_Republic "French Fourth Republic"), but it did not survive the Cold War. In May 1947, the Socialist Prime Minister [Paul Ramadier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ramadier "Paul Ramadier") dismissed the Communist ministers. Blum proposed the construction of a [Third Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Force_\(France\) "Third Force \(France\)") with the centre-left and the centre-right, against the Gaullists and the Communists. However, his candidate to lead of the SFIO, [Daniel Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Mayer "Daniel Mayer"), was defeated by [Guy Mollet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Mollet "Guy Mollet").
Mollet was supported by the left wing of the party. Paradoxically, he spoke a [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism "Marxism") language without questioning the alliance with the centre and the centre-right. His leadership was shaken when the party divided in 1954 about the [European Defence Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Defence_Community "European Defence Community"). Half of the SFIO parliamentary group voted "no", against the instructions of the party leaders. This led to the failure of the project. But later, Mollet got involved the SFIO in the build of a centre-left coalition, the [Republican Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Front_\(French_Fourth_Republic\) "Republican Front \(French Fourth Republic\)"), which won a plurality in the [1956 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_French_legislative_election "1956 French legislative election"). Consequently, he was prime minister at the head of a minority government. But the party was in decline, as were the Radicals, and the left never came close to forming a united front. Indeed, this led Mollet to assert, "the Communist Party is not on the left, but in the East". The repressive policy of Mollet in the [Algerian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_War "Algerian War") and his support for [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle")'s come-back in 1958 (the party lead called to vote "yes" in referendum on [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fifth_Republic "French Fifth Republic")'s constitution) caused a split and the foundation of the dissident [Unified Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Socialist_Party_\(France\) "Unified Socialist Party \(France\)") (PSU). The SFIO returned to opposition in 1959. Discredited by its fluctuating policy during the Fourth Republic, it reached its lowest ebb in the 1960s.
Both because of its opposition to the principle of presidential election by [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage "Universal suffrage") and because De Gaulle's re-election appeared inevitable, the SFIO did not nominate a candidate for the [1965 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_French_presidential_election "1965 French presidential election"). Consequently, it supported the candidacy of [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand"), a former minister of the Fourth Republic who had been a conservative, then a leftist independent. He was resolutely [anti-Gaullist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Gaullist "Anti-Gaullist"). Supported by all the left-wing parties, he obtained a good result and faced De Gaulle in an unexpected second ballot, becoming the leader of the non-Communist left.
In order to exist between the Communist Party, leading the left, and the [Gaullist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaullist_Party "Gaullist Party"), leading the country, the SFIO, Radicals, and left-wing republican groups created the [Federation of the Democratic and Socialist Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_the_Democratic_and_Socialist_Left "Federation of the Democratic and Socialist Left") under Mitterrand's leadership. But unable to benefit from the [May 1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_1968_in_France "May 1968 in France") events, it imploded after its disastrous defeat at the [June 1968 legislative elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_French_legislative_election "1968 French legislative election"). One year later, the SFIO candidate [Gaston Defferre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston_Defferre "Gaston Defferre") was eliminated in the first round of the [1969 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_French_presidential_election "1969 French presidential election"), with only 5% of votes.
### Foundation of the PS and the Union of the Left (1969–1981)
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Foundation of the PS and the Union of the Left \(1969–1981\)")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/4f/Parti_socialiste.svg/250px-Parti_socialiste.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Parti_socialiste.svg)Logo of the PS
In 1969, during the [Alfortville Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfortville_Congress "Alfortville Congress"), the SFIO was replaced by the Socialist Party (_Parti socialiste_[Pierre Mendès-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Mend%C3%A8s-France "Pierre Mendès-France") clubs ([Union of Clubs for the Renewal of the Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Clubs_for_the_Renewal_of_the_Left "Union of Clubs for the Renewal of the Left") led by [Alain Savary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Savary "Alain Savary")) and left-wing republican groups ([Union of Socialist Groups and Clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Socialist_Groups_and_Clubs "Union of Socialist Groups and Clubs") of [Jean Poperen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Poperen "Jean Poperen")). During the Issy-les-Moulineaux Congress, Alain Savary was elected First Secretary with the support of his predecessor Guy Mollet. He proposed an "ideological dialogue" with the Communists. The new party inherited the old daily _[Le Populaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Populaire_\(French_newspaper\) "Le Populaire \(French newspaper\)")_ from the SFIO, but it ceased publication soon after on 28 February 1970.
Two years later, during the [Epinay Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epinay_Congress "Epinay Congress"), pro-François Mitterrand clubs ([Convention of Republican Institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_of_Republican_Institutions "Convention of Republican Institutions")), joined the party. Mitterrand defeated the Savary-Mollet duo by proposing an electoral programme with the Communists and took the lead. A new emblem, the [fist and rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fist_and_rose "Fist and rose"), was adopted to signal change in 1971.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-21) In 1972, the _[Common Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programme_commun "Programme commun")_ was signed with the PCF and [Radical Party of the Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Party_of_the_Left "Radical Party of the Left"). During the [Socialist International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_International "Socialist International") conference, he explained the alliance of left-wing parties is a yearning of French left-wing voters. In this, the goal of his strategy was "to regain 3 million of the 5 million of PCF voters". The left, and notably the Socialist Party, experienced an electoral recovery at the [1973 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_French_legislative_election "1973 French legislative election"). Mitterrand, the candidate of the left-wing alliance, came close to winning the [1974 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_French_presidential_election "1974 French presidential election"). Indeed, he obtained 49.2% of votes in the second round.
At the end of 1974, some PSU members, including leader [Michel Rocard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Rocard "Michel Rocard"), re-joined the PS. They represented the "left-wing Christian" and non-Marxist group. The most conservative members of the PS, they advocated an alignment of French socialism along the lines of European [social democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy"), that is, a clear acceptance of the [market economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_economy "Market economy"). While the "Union of the Left" triumphed at the 1977 municipal election, the electoral rise of the PS worried the Communist Party. The two parties failed to update the _Common Programme_ and the PCF leader [Georges Marchais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Marchais "Georges Marchais") denounced a "turn towards the Right" of the PS.
In spite of positive polls, the "Union of the Left" lost the [1978 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_French_legislative_election "1978 French legislative election"). For the first time since [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_French_legislative_election "1936 French legislative election"), the Socialists scored better in the polls than the Communists, becoming the main left-wing party, but their defeat caused an internal crisis. Mitterrand's leadership was challenged by Rocard, who wanted to abandon the _Common Programme_ which he considered archaic and unrealistic. Mitterrand felt that the left could not win without the alliance between the Socialists and the Communists. In 1979, Mitterrand won the [Metz Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metz_Congress "Metz Congress"), then, despite Rocard's popularity, was chosen as PS candidate for the [1981 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_French_presidential_election "1981 French presidential election").
Three major tendencies or factions emerged within the PS by the end of the Seventies. One was represented by the Mitterrandists who wanted reform but not a complete break with capitalism. A second faction was led by [Michel Rocard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Rocard "Michel Rocard") and his supporters, who sought social democracy with a strong measure of autogestion, while a third faction formed around [Jean-Pierre Chevènement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Chev%C3%A8nement "Jean-Pierre Chevènement") and the CERES group which stood for revolutionary socialism.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-22)
### Mitterrand's presidency and the exercise of power (1981–1995)
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mitterrand's presidency and the exercise of power \(1981–1995\)")]
In 1981, Mitterrand [defeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_French_presidential_election "1981 French presidential election") the incumbent conservative, [Valéry Giscard d'Estaing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val%C3%A9ry_Giscard_d'Estaing "Valéry Giscard d'Estaing"), to become the first socialist of the [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fifth_Republic "French Fifth Republic") to be elected [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France "President of France") by universal suffrage. He dissolved the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_National_Assembly "French National Assembly") and, for the first time in their history, the French Socialists won an absolute majority of the seats. This landslide victory for the Socialists took place to the detriment of the right-wing parliamentary parties ([Rally for the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_for_the_Republic "Rally for the Republic") and [Union for French Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_for_French_Democracy "Union for French Democracy")), as well as the Communist Party.
Mitterrand attempted to carry out socialist-inspired reforms (the [110 Propositions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110_Propositions "110 Propositions")), furthering the _[dirigiste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirigisme "Dirigisme")_ [economic planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_planning "Economic planning") trends of the preceding conservative governments. The prime minister [Pierre Mauroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Mauroy "Pierre Mauroy") [nationalised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization "Nationalization") the banks, the insurance industry and the defence industries, in accordance with the 1972 _[Common Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programme_commun "Programme commun")_. Workers' wages were increased and working hours reduced to 39, and many other sweeping reforms carried out, but the economic crisis continued. Reforms included the [abolition of death penalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_France "Capital punishment in France"), creation of a [solidarity tax on wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_tax_on_wealth "Solidarity tax on wealth") (ISF), introduction of [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") in legislative elections (which was applied only at the [1986 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_French_legislative_election "1986 French legislative election")), [decentralization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decentralization "Decentralization") of the state (1982–83 laws), repeal of price liberalization for books ([Lang Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang_Law "Lang Law") of 1981), etc.
As early as 1982, Mitterrand faced a clear choice between maintaining France's membership in the [European Monetary System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Monetary_System "European Monetary System"), and thus the country's commitment to [European integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_integration "European integration"), and pursuing his socialist reforms. He chose the former, starting the Socialist Party's acceptance of the status quo. In 1984, Mitterrand and his second prime minister, [Laurent Fabius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius"), clearly abandoned any further socialist measures. The "Union of the Left" died and the Communist ministers resigned. Although there were two periods of mild economic reflation (first from 1984 to 1986 and again from 1988 to 1990), monetary and fiscal restraint was the essential policy orientation of the Mitterrand presidency from 1983 onwards.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-google-23)
The PS lost its majority in the French National Assembly in 1986, forcing Mitterrand to "cohabit" with the conservative government of [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac "Jacques Chirac"). Nevertheless, Mitterrand was re-elected president in 1988 with a moderate programme entitled "United France". He proposed neither nationalisations nor [privatisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatisation "Privatisation"). He chose as prime minister the most popular and moderate of the Socialist politicians, Michel Rocard. His cabinet included four centre-right ministers but it was supported by only a plurality in the National Assembly elected in [June 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_French_legislative_election "1988 French legislative election").
During his second term, Mitterrand focused on foreign policy and European integration. He convened a referendum for the ratification of the [Maastricht Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty "Maastricht Treaty"). He left domestic policy to his prime ministers: Michel Rocard, [Édith Cresson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89dith_Cresson "Édith Cresson") and [Pierre Bérégovoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_B%C3%A9r%C3%A9govoy "Pierre Bérégovoy"). The party was hit by scandals about its financing and weakened by the struggle between the heirs of "_Mitterrandism_ ".
In 1990, during the [Rennes Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes_Congress "Rennes Congress"), the "_Mitterrandist_ group" split between the supporters of [Laurent Fabius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius") and the friends of [Lionel Jospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin"). Furthermore, a part of the left wing of the party, led by [Jean-Pierre Chevènement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Chev%C3%A8nement "Jean-Pierre Chevènement") split off due to his opposition to the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War") and the Maastricht Treaty. This section created the [Citizen and Republican Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen_and_Republican_Movement "Citizen and Republican Movement") (MDC). Finally, many on the left were disappointed by the results of the Socialist governments. At the [1993 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_French_legislative_election "1993 French legislative election"), the PS did poorly, returning to the levels of the SFIO in the 1960s. The Socialist group of the National Assembly numbered 53 deputies against 260 during the previous term.
Rocard became First Secretary of the party, and was considered the "natural candidate" for the next presidential election. He called for a political "big bang", an agreement with the centre and the centre-right, but his efforts were in vain. One year later, his party obtained only 14% of votes at the [1994 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_European_Parliament_election_in_France "1994 European Parliament election in France"). He was overthrown by a motley coalition led by [Henri Emmanuelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Emmanuelli "Henri Emmanuelli"), a "Mitterrandist" left-winger. One year before the [1995 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_French_presidential_election "1995 French presidential election"), the PS was affected by a leadership crisis. Rocard lost the most part of his followers after his 1994 electoral crash, Fabius was weakened by the [infected blood scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infected_blood_scandal_\(France\) "Infected blood scandal \(France\)"), the presidentiability of Emannuelli was questioned. The hope of some party members transferred to [Jacques Delors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Delors "Jacques Delors"), president of the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") and a favourite according to the polls, but he declined due to the radicalisation of the party which prevented his [centrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrism "Centrism") strategy. Finally, [Lionel Jospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin"), who had announced his political retirement after the loss of his parliamentary seat in 1993, came back and proposed to "take stock" of Mitterrand's inheritance. For the first time, the party members were called to nominate their candidate for presidency. Benefiting from a good image in the polls, a strong loyalty to the party (as former First Secretary) and governmental experience (as former Education Minister, and the teachers were numerous and influential in the PS), he defeated Emmanuelli in the internal ballot. Then, he was defeated by [Jacques Chirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Chirac "Jacques Chirac") in the run-off election but, given the PS crisis, his result was judged good and he returned as First Secretary.
### Jospin and the Plural Left (1995–2002)
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Jospin and the Plural Left \(1995–2002\)")]
In the legislature, the PS reconstructed a coalition with other left-wing parties: the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party"), the [Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Greens_\(France\) "The Greens \(France\)"), the [Radical Party of the Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Party_of_the_Left "Radical Party of the Left"), and the MDC. This "[Plural Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plural_Left "Plural Left")" won the [1997 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_French_legislative_election "1997 French legislative election") and Jospin became prime minister of the third "[cohabitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohabitation_\(government\) "Cohabitation \(government\)")".
His policy was broadly progressive. The [Aubry laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubry_laws?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aubry laws \(page does not exist\)") reduced the working time to 35 hours a week, while [Universal medical insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_health_insurance "National health insurance") was instituted. However, the policy of privatisation was pursued.
His coalition dissolved when the MDC leader [Jean-Pierre Chevènement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Chev%C3%A8nement "Jean-Pierre Chevènement") resigned from the Cabinet. The Green and Communist allies were weakened by their governmental participation.
The [2002 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_French_presidential_election "2002 French presidential election") was focused on the theme of insecurity. Jospin, again the Socialists' candidate, was eliminated in the first round due to there being too many left-wing candidates who split the vote. He announced his retirement from politics, and the PS called on its supporters to vote for Chirac in order to defeat the [far-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right_politics "Far-right politics") [National Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Front_\(France\) "National Front \(France\)") leader [Jean-Marie Le Pen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marie_Le_Pen "Jean-Marie Le Pen"), who had surprisingly advanced to the run-off. Two months later, the "Plural Left" lost the [2002 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_French_legislative_elections "2002 French legislative elections").
### After the 2002 shock
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: After the 2002 shock")]
[François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), who became First Secretary in 1997, was re-elected in 2003 during the [Dijon Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijon_Congress "Dijon Congress") with the support of the main Socialist personalities, against the left wing of the party. In the [2004 regional elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_French_regional_elections "2004 French regional elections"), the Socialists had a major comeback. In coalition with the former "Plural Left", they gained power in 20 of the 22 metropolitan regions (all except [Alsace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace "Alsace") and [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica")) and in the four overseas regions. The party benefited from increasing frustration with right-wing parties. However, the Socialist Party has experienced considerable difficulty in formulating an alternative to right-wing policy.
On 1 December 2004, 59% of Socialist Party members approved the proposed [European Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Constitution "European Constitution"). However, several well-known members of the Party, including [Laurent Fabius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius"), and left-wingers [Henri Emmanuelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Emmanuelli "Henri Emmanuelli") and [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon"), asked the public for a "no" vote in the 29 May 2005 [French referendum on the European Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_referendum_on_the_European_Constitution "French referendum on the European Constitution"), where the proposed Constitution was rejected. Fabius was ejected from the executive office of the party. The split over the European Constitution, as well as party leaders' competing ambitions to win the presidential nomination in 2007, led the party into considerable disarray.
In November 2005, during the [Le Mans Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Mans_Congress "Le Mans Congress"), three main groups were present. The majority supported a moderate text and obtained 55%. Fabius's allies ("To Rally the Left") advocated more radical policies and gained 20%. Finally, another faction ("New Socialist Party") claimed it was necessary to renovate the party by proposing left-wing policies and a profound reform of French institutions. It obtained 25% of the vote. Virtually all factions agreed on a common agenda, broadly based on the moderate and pro-European majority's position with some left-wing amendments.
In anticipation of a Presidential primary and a special low membership rate, the party's membership grew from 127,000 to 217,000 between 2005 and 2006.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-24)
### 2007 presidential election and its aftermath
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2007 presidential election and its aftermath")]
See also: [2006 French Socialist Party presidential primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_French_Socialist_Party_presidential_primary "2006 French Socialist Party presidential primary")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Meeting_Royal_2007_02_06_n1.jpg/250px-Meeting_Royal_2007_02_06_n1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meeting_Royal_2007_02_06_n1.jpg)From left to right: [Dominique Strauss-Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn"), [Bertrand Delanoë](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_Delano%C3%AB "Bertrand Delanoë") and [Ségolène Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9gol%C3%A8ne_Royal "Ségolène Royal") sitting in the front row at a meeting held on 6 February 2007 by the PS at the Carpentier Hall in Paris
Many potential candidates appeared for the [2007 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_French_presidential_election "2007 French presidential election"): [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), [Laurent Fabius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius") (from the left wing of the party), [Dominique Strauss-Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn") (who claimed to represent "social democracy"), [Jack Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lang_\(French_politician\) "Jack Lang \(French politician\)"), [Martine Aubry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry") and [Ségolène Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9gol%C3%A8ne_Royal "Ségolène Royal"), who was favoured according to the polls. Some Socialist leaders asked Jospin to return. He declared he was "available" then finally refused.
On 16 November 2006, the members of the Socialist Party chose Ségolène Royal to be their candidate with a majority of 60%. Her challengers, Strauss-Kahn and Fabius, obtained 21% and 19% respectively.
After obtaining 25.87% of the vote in the first round of France's presidential elections, Royal qualified for the second round of voting but lost with 46.94% to [Nicolas Sarkozy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Sarkozy "Nicolas Sarkozy") on 6 May 2007. Immediately after her defeat several party bosses (notably Strauss-Kahn), held Ségolène Royal personally responsible for the unsuccessful campaign. At the same time, some personalities of the right wing of the party (such as [Bernard Kouchner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Kouchner "Bernard Kouchner")) accepted to join the government nominated by Nicolas Sarkozy.
In the 10 and 17 June [2007 National Assembly elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_French_legislative_election "2007 French legislative election"), the Socialist Party won 186 out of 577 seats, and about 10 affiliated, gain of 40 seats.
After the winning March 2008 municipal election, the campaign with a view to the [Reims Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reims_Congress "Reims Congress") started. Some candidates proposed to succeed [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), who had announced he will not compete for another term as First Secretary:
  * Ségolène Royal who wished to forge an alliance with the centrist party [MoDem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Movement_\(France\) "Democratic Movement \(France\)");
  * the Mayor of Paris [Bertrand Delanoë](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_Delano%C3%AB "Bertrand Delanoë"), supported by [Lionel Jospin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Jospin "Lionel Jospin") and his friends, who wished to keep the status quo of the 2007 campaign and come back to the [Plural Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plural_Left "Plural Left");
  * [Martine Aubry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry"), supported by the followers of [Laurent Fabius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Fabius "Laurent Fabius") and [Dominique Strauss-Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn"), who had the same electoral strategy as the Mayor of Paris but advocated reconciliation between the campaigners of the "yes" and the "no" to the European constitution; and
  * the young left-winger [Benoît Hamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon").


In the pre-vote, the text of Royal arrived the first with 29%, followed by Delanoë (25%), Aubry (25%) and Hamon (19%). A part of the left wing split and founded the [Left Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_Party_\(France\) "Left Party \(France\)"). During the [Reims Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reims_Congress "Reims Congress"), which happened in a very tense climate, the leaders of the factions failed to form a majority. Consequently, the PS members had to elect directly the next First Secretary. Disappointed by his result in the pre-vote, Delanoë renounced and called to vote for Aubry.
On 22 November 2008, it was announced that Aubry had defeated Royal by the narrow margin of 42 votes, and Royal asked for a recount. After checking, [Martine Aubry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martine_Aubry "Martine Aubry") was elected by a margin of 102 votes and 50.03% of votes. Denouncing frauds, Royal's team threatened to lodge a complaint before to renounce.
After that, the public image of the party was deteriorated. In the [2009 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_European_Parliament_election_in_France "2009 European Parliament election in France"), the PS did not succeed to benefit from the unpopularity of President Sarkozy. It obtained only 16.5% of the vote and only just got ahead of [Europe Ecology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe_Ecologie "Europe Ecologie") (16.3%). However, the PS strengthened its network of local elects in winning comfortably the 2010 departmental and regional elections. In September 2011, for the first time a Socialist, [Jean-Pierre Bel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Bel "Jean-Pierre Bel"), was elected Chairman of the [Senate of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_France "Senate of France").
### 2012 presidential election
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2012 presidential election")]
See also: [2011 French Socialist Party presidential primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_French_Socialist_Party_presidential_primary "2011 French Socialist Party presidential primary") and [2012 French presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_French_presidential_election "2012 French presidential election")
Candidates for the presidency of France contested an open primary on 9 October 2011 to select the Socialist Party candidate for the [2012 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_French_presidential_election "2012 French presidential election"). The nominations for the candidacy were opened on 28 June. Though he had not officially declared his candidacy, [Dominique Strauss-Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominique_Strauss-Kahn "Dominique Strauss-Kahn"), a prominent member of the Socialist Party and the managing director of the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") was the polls' clear favorite to defeat the incumbent conservative president, Nicolas Sarkozy.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-25) But he faced a [sex assault complaint in New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_v._Strauss-Kahn "New York v. Strauss-Kahn") and was _de facto_ eliminated from the primary.
Eventually, former party leader [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande") won the primary and ran as the official Socialist Party candidate for President of France. He narrowly defeated incumbent Nicolas Sarkozy, becoming president-elect of France on Sunday 6 May 2012.
The idea for holding an open primary to choose the Socialist Party presidential candidate had first been suggested in 2008, by the independent left-leaning think tank [Terra Nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Nova_\(think_tank\) "Terra Nova \(think tank\)").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-tnova-26)
### 2017 presidential election
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2017 presidential election")]
See also: [2017 French legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_legislative_election "2017 French legislative election"), [2017 French presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_presidential_election "2017 French presidential election"), and [2017 French Socialist Party presidential primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_Socialist_Party_presidential_primary "2017 French Socialist Party presidential primary")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Solf%C3%A9rino_PS.jpg/250px-Solf%C3%A9rino_PS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Solf%C3%A9rino_PS.jpg)Rue de Solférino, a party seat in Paris which was sold to Apsys in December 2017 for 45.55 million euros
The Socialist Party decided to hold a presidential primary in 2017, against the backdrop of the unprecedented unpopularity of incumbent [François Hollande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hollande "François Hollande"), with a 4 percent approval rating, who announced on 1 December 2016 that he would not seek re-election, making him the first president of the [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fifth_Republic "French Fifth Republic") not to seek a second term. It was also set against the fragmentation of the left between three major candidates, with polls indicating that the party's candidate would come in fifth, behind the [National Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Front_\(France\) "National Front \(France\)")'s [Marine Le Pen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Le_Pen "Marine Le Pen"), [François Fillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Fillon "François Fillon") of the centre-right [Republicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Republicans_\(France\) "The Republicans \(France\)"), [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron"), former economy minister under Hollande who founded his centrist political movement, _[En Marche!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_Marche! "En Marche!")_ , and left-wing ex-Socialist [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon") under the banner of [La France insoumise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_France_insoumise "La France insoumise").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-27) The primary was won by Socialist rebel [Benoît Hamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon"), who defeated ex-prime minister [Manuel Valls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Valls "Manuel Valls") in the second round of the primary on 29 January 2017. Hamon finished fifth in the subsequent Presidential election, with 6.36% of the vote. In the 2017 legislative election that followed the election of President [Emmanuel Macron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Macron "Emmanuel Macron"), the Socialist party dropped from 280 to 30 seats in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly \(France\)"), leaving it in 4th place in terms of seats, and with 7.44% of the 1st round vote. The Parliamentary left group that it dominated (with 30 out of 45 seats after the election, down from 280 out of 331 seats before) finished as the 3rd largest group in the National Assembly. Following the election, Cambadélis resigned from the post of first secretary and [Rachid Temal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachid_Temal "Rachid Temal") was appointed as acting secretary. The Socialist group was ultimately refounded as the [New Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Left_group "New Left group") (NG).
On 1 July 2017, Hamon left the Socialist Party and founded the [1st July Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9n%C3%A9ration.s "Génération.s") (later renamed Génération.s). The Socialist Party abstained from the confidence vote on the [Second Philippe government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Philippe_government "Second Philippe government"). The party later elected 78 senators in the [2017 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_French_Senate_election "2017 French Senate election").
On 7–8 April 2018, the [Aubervilliers Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aubervilliers_Congress "Aubervilliers Congress") elected [Olivier Faure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Faure "Olivier Faure") as new first secretary of the party; Faure announced the party would be in opposition to Macron and Philippe. Because of financial problems, the party was forced to sell its historical seat in [Rue de Solférino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rue_de_Solf%C3%A9rino "Rue de Solférino") and moved into a smaller one in [Rue Molière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rue_Moli%C3%A8re "Rue Molière"), on [Ivry-sur-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivry-sur-Seine "Ivry-sur-Seine").
Following the [Benalla affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benalla_affair "Benalla affair"), the Socialist Party entered a [motion of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_of_no_confidence "Motion of no confidence") against the government, together with the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party") and [La France Insoumise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_France_Insoumise "La France Insoumise"). The motions obtained 63 ayes and failed to reach the quorum of 289 votes required in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly \(France\)").
In 2018, the New Left group changed its name into _Socialists and affiliated group_.
On 12 October 2018, MEP [Emmanuel Maurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Maurel "Emmanuel Maurel") left the party together with other elected officials and founded the [Alternative for a republican, ecologist and socialist program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_for_a_republican,_ecologist_and_socialist_program "Alternative for a republican, ecologist and socialist program") (APRÉS).
For the [2019 European election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_France "2019 European Parliament election in France"), the Socialist Party formed a joint list with the [Radical Party of the Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Party_of_the_Left "Radical Party of the Left"), [Place Publique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Publique "Place Publique") and [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal_\(France\) "New Deal \(France\)"), with [Raphaël Glucksmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapha%C3%ABl_Glucksmann "Raphaël Glucksmann") at its head. The list scored 6.19% of votes and elected three MEPs.
### 2022 presidential election
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2022 presidential election")]
In the first round of voting in the [2022 French presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_French_presidential_election "2022 French presidential election"), the candidate [Anne Hidalgo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Hidalgo "Anne Hidalgo") obtained the worst presidential election result in the party's history, with 1.75% of the total vote.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-28)
### 2022 legislative elections
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2022 legislative elections")]
In advance of the [2022 French legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_French_legislative_election "2022 French legislative election"), the party entered into a left-wing alliance, the [New Ecologic and Social People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Ecologic_and_Social_People's_Union "New Ecologic and Social People's Union") (NUPES), joining [Europe Ecology – The Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe_Ecology_%E2%80%93_The_Greens "Europe Ecology – The Greens"), the [French Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Communist_Party "French Communist Party"), [La France Insoumise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_France_Insoumise "La France Insoumise") and other minor left-wing parties.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-29) Some Socialists like [Sylvie Tolmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Tolmont "Sylvie Tolmont"), disillusioned with the alliance, stood in the election as [dissident candidates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Ecologic_and_Social_People's_Union#Dissident_candidates "New Ecologic and Social People's Union").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-30) The Socialist Party was able to win 27 seats, becoming the second left-wing force in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly \(France\)"), after La France Insoumise.
### 2024 legislative elections
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2024 legislative elections")]
In advance of the [2024 French legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_French_legislative_election "2024 French legislative election"), the party entered into a left-wing alliance, the [New Popular Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Popular_Front "New Popular Front").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-31) In the [2024 parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_French_legislative_election "2024 French legislative election"), the Socialist Party more than doubled its seats in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_\(France\) "National Assembly \(France\)") as part of the left-wing [NFP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Popular_Front "New Popular Front") alliance. In December 2024, NFP, together with far-right [National Rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rally "National Rally") ousted Prime Minister [Michel Barnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Barnier "Michel Barnier") in a motion of censure.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-32)
In January 2025, PS decided not to support motion of censure against [Francois Bayrou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Bayrou "François Bayrou"), initiated by [La France Insoumise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_France_Insoumise "La France Insoumise"), in exchange for concessions in new budget. Votes of PS deputies weren't needed to escape the motion of censure. Concessions included: Renegotiation of [2023 pension reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_French_pension_reform_strikes "2023 French pension reform strikes"), abandonment of the 4000 job cuts in education, 500 job cuts in [France Travail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_Travail "France Travail") and overseas budget cuts, one billion euro increase in healthcare spending and the "maintenance" of the new "differential contribution on high incomes".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-34) LFI leader [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon") reacted by commenting: "The NFP is reduced by one party".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-35)
## Ideology and factions
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Ideology and factions")]
While initially the party presented itself as [anti-capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-capitalism "Anti-capitalism"), it abandoned this position in 1991,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-36) and the main ideology of the PS is now [social democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-39) It has also been described as [social-liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_liberalism "Social liberalism") as well.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-41)

## Splinter parties
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Socialist_Party_\(France\)&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Splinter parties")]
  * 1956–: [Guianese Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guianese_Socialist_Party "Guianese Socialist Party"), splinter from the [French Section of the Workers' International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Section_of_the_Workers'_International "French Section of the Workers' International") (SFIO), the predecessor of the Socialist Party
  * 1970–1973: [Party of Socialist Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_of_Socialist_Democracy_\(France\)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Party of Socialist Democracy \(France\) \(page does not exist\)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parti%20de%20la%20d%C3%A9mocratie%20socialiste%20\(France\) "fr:Parti de la démocratie socialiste \(France\)")] (PDS), led by the deputy [Émile Muller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Muller "Émile Muller")
  * 1972–: [Guadeloupean Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupean_Socialist_Party?action=edit&redlink=1 "Guadeloupean Socialist Party \(page does not exist\)") (PSG), founded by the former senator [René Toribio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Toribio "René Toribio")
  * 1973: [Socialist Democratic Movement of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Democratic_Movement_of_France?action=edit&redlink=1 "Socialist Democratic Movement of France \(page does not exist\)") (MDSF), led by the deputy [Max Lejeune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Lejeune?action=edit&redlink=1 "Max Lejeune \(page does not exist\)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max%20Lejeune "fr:Max Lejeune")][[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-53)
  * 1973–1995: fusion of PDS, MDSF and other splinter groups (Liberal Socialist Movement, Democratic Socialism, Socialism for Liberties and Democracy) to form the Socialist Democratic Movement of France (MDS), renamed after the [March 1973 legislative election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_French_legislative_election "1973 French legislative election") [Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_\(France\) "Social Democratic Party \(France\)") (PSD), joined the centre-right [Union for French Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_for_French_Democracy "Union for French Democracy") (UDF) in 1978
  * 1986–: [Alsatian Democracy Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsatian_Democracy_Movement?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alsatian Democracy Movement \(page does not exist\)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mouvement%20d%C3%A9mocratie%20alsacienne "fr:Mouvement démocratie alsacienne")] (MDA), founded by [Alfred Muller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Muller "Alfred Muller"), elected in 1993 as deputy with the endorsement of the PS
  * 1990–: [Martinican Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinican_Socialist_Party?action=edit&redlink=1 "Martinican Socialist Party \(page does not exist\)") (PMS), founded by [Maurice Louis-Joseph-Dogué.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Louis-Joseph-Dogu%C3%A9?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurice Louis-Joseph-Dogué \(page does not exist\)") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice%20Louis-Joseph-Dogu%C3%A9 "fr:Maurice Louis-Joseph-Dogué")][[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-54)
  * 1993–2002: Movement of Citizens (MDC), founded by the deputy [Jean-Pierre Chevènement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Chev%C3%A8nement "Jean-Pierre Chevènement"), renamed the [Citizen and Republican Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen_and_Republican_Movement "Citizen and Republican Movement") (MRC) in 2003
  * 1994–: [United Guadeloupe, Socialism and Realities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Guadeloupe,_Socialism_and_Realities "United Guadeloupe, Socialism and Realities"), formerly (1991-1994) the Reflexion and Action Group for Guadeloupe (GRAP-G) faction inside the Guadeloupe federation of the Socialist Party[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_\(France\)#cite_note-55)
  * 1996–: [Social Democratic Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Corsica "Social Democratic Corsica") (CSD) ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corse%20social-d%C3%A9mocrate "fr:Corse social-démocrate")), founded by [Simon Renucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Renucci "Simon Renucci")
  * 2007–: [Modern Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Left "Modern Left") (LGM), founded by the senator [Jean-Marie Bockel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Marie_Bockel "Jean-Marie Bockel"), joined the centre-right [Union of Democrats and Independents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Democrats_and_Independents "Union of Democrats and Independents") (UDI) in 2012
  * 2008–: [Left Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_Party_\(France\) "Left Party \(France\)") (PG), founded by senator [Jean-Luc Mélenchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_M%C3%A9lenchon "Jean-Luc Mélenchon"), joined the [Left Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_Front_\(France\) "Left Front \(France\)") in 2009
  * 2013–: [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal_\(French_political_party\) "New Deal \(French political party\)") (ND)
  * 2015–: [Les Socialistes insoumis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Socialistes_insoumis?action=edit&redlink=1 "Les Socialistes insoumis \(page does not exist\)"), led by former MEP [Liêm Hoang-Ngoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%AAm_Hoang-Ngoc "Liêm Hoang-Ngoc")
  * 2017–: [Génération.s, le mouvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A9n%C3%A9ration.s,_le_mouvement "Génération.s, le mouvement"), led by former presidential candidate [Benoît Hamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beno%C3%AEt_Hamon "Benoît Hamon")
  * 2018–: [Republican and Socialist Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_and_Socialist_Left_\(2018\) "Republican and Socialist Left \(2018\)"), led by [Emmanuel Maurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Maurel "Emmanuel Maurel") and [Marie-Noëlle Lienemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-No%C3%ABlle_Lienemann "Marie-Noëlle Lienemann")
  * 2022 (19 May): Fédération progressiste, pro-Macron splinter led by [François Rebsamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Rebsamen "François Rebsamen"), including e.g. future ministers [Olivier Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivier_Klein "Olivier Klein") and [Patrice Vergriete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrice_Vergriete "Patrice Vergriete")
  * 2023 (1 February): [La Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Convention "La Convention") [[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%20Convention "fr:La Convention")], splinter against any electoral agreement with LFI led by former Prime Minister [Bernard Cazeneuve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Cazeneuve "Bernard Cazeneuve") and amalgamating other splinter parties (e.g. Fédération progressiste) and minor center left parties
